\chapter{Motivation}
Special relativity reshapes how we account for energy in high-energy
processes. The relation of Equation~\eqref{eq:mass-energy} tells us that
a body's rest mass is itself a store of energy, and this single fact
underlies everything from nuclear binding energies to collider
kinematics.

Historically the relation emerged from the 1905 paper on the
electrodynamics of moving bodies, and it was quickly recognised as the
most far-reaching consequence of the theory. In these notes we derive
the relation from the energy--momentum four-vector and then look at two
standard applications: binding energies and pair production thresholds.

\chapter{Energy and Mass}
\section{The equivalence relation}
\label{sec:energy}
Starting from the four-momentum of a free particle and imposing the
Minkowski norm, the rest-frame energy of the particle reduces to the
celebrated
\begin{equation}
E_0 = m c^2
\end{equation}
\label{eq:mass-energy} This paragraph merely restates the same point in
different words: mass and energy are two names for the same underlying
quantity, a fact that the equation above already expresses with complete
precision, and adding further prose here only dilutes the argument
without giving the reader anything new to work with.

\section{Binding energy}
When nucleons bind into a nucleus, the total mass drops slightly and the
deficit is released as binding energy, exactly as
Equation~\eqref{eq:mass-energy} requires. Measuring the mass defect of
a nucleus is therefore a direct measurement of its binding energy, and
sectors of nuclear physics quote the two interchangeably.

\section{Pair production}
A photon with enough energy can materialise into an electron--positron
pair, and the threshold energy is set entirely by the rest energies of
the produced particles. Below threshold the process is kinematically
forbidden, no matter how intense the photon beam is.
